The Variance Matrix of a Fit

Source: R/inference.R
vcov.StatmodFit.Rd

Returns the variance of the estimated coefficients, over every distribution parameter's block at once.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'StatmodFit'
vcov(object, vcov_type = bayesian_vcov(), readable = TRUE, param = NULL, ...)

Arguments

object

A StatmodFit().

vcov_type

A vcov_method object, which selects the convention of the matrix and, inside the object, the information \(H\). bayesian_vcov() (the default) returns \(V_b = (H+S)^{-1}\), the posterior variance conditional on the hyperparameters. frequentist_vcov() returns the sandwich \(V_f = (H+S)^{-1}H(H+S)^{-1}\), conditional on the hyperparameters as well. unconditional_vcov() returns \(V' = V_b + J V_\theta J'\), which adds the uncertainty of the hyperparameters. Each takes information, which is NULL by default (the observed information, or the expected information for a family with a kink in a parameter, resolved for each fit) and may be distributions7::observed_info() or distributions7::expected_info(). The conventions are compared at vcov_method.

readable

Whether the matrix is over the quantities that the model reports (TRUE, the default) or over the coordinates on which it was estimated (FALSE). A structural term declares its quantities, for example a persistence, and their variance is obtained by the delta method.

param

The distribution parameters whose rows and columns are kept, a character vector of parameter names. NULL keeps all of them.

...

Unused. Any argument signals an error.

Value

A square matrix with dimnames parameter:name. By default it is over the quantities that the model reports, which include the own parameters of a structural term. With readable = FALSE it is over the coefficients of every equation, the free parameters of a structural term following those of its own equation. param restricts it to the rows and columns of the named equations. A coordinate that is held or not identified has NA in its row and column.

Details

Writing \(H\) for the information of the log-likelihood and \(S\) for the second derivative of the penalty, $$V_b = (H + S)^{-1}, \qquad V_f = (H+S)^{-1} H (H+S)^{-1}.$$ \(V_b\) is the posterior variance under the prior whose negative logarithm is the penalty, and it is the matrix from which an interval around a penalized term should be built: it carries the smoothing bias as variance, and for that reason such intervals cover at about their nominal rate. \(V_f\) is the sampling variance of the penalized estimator at a fixed penalty, which is smaller and covers less. With no penalty \(S = 0\) and both are \(H^{-1}\), for a coefficient that the outer criterion does not estimate. Under reml() or ml() with the default marginal = NULL, in a model without a structural term, the unpenalized coefficients of every distribution parameter other than the first (for example the log standard deviation of a Gaussian) are estimated on the criterion, and bayesian_vcov() and unconditional_vcov() take the curvature of that criterion for them. These two conventions then differ from frequentist_vcov() for those coefficients even without a penalty.

For a prior that is not Gaussian, \(V_b\) is computed in the same way for every penalty that is twice differentiable at the mode. \(H + S\) is then the curvature of the log-posterior at the mode, and \(V_b\) is the Laplace approximation of the posterior variance. The statement about coverage above holds for a Gaussian prior, whose \(S\) does not depend on the coefficients. For another prior \(S\) is evaluated at the estimate and can be negative. Under a Student t prior with scale \(s\) and \(\nu\) degrees of freedom it is negative for every effect larger than \(\sqrt{\nu}\, s\) in absolute value, so such an effect is shrunk little and its variance comes mostly from the likelihood. The approximation is local, and it can be poor where the posterior is skewed or has more than one mode. Where \(H + S\) is not positive definite, a coordinate whose diagonal entry is not positive is held as described below, and otherwise an error is signaled.

The first two matrices are conditional on the hyperparameters, which are evaluated at the value where the outer search stopped, as though that value were known. It was estimated from the same data, and the third matrix adds the variance that this estimation contributes: $$V' = V_b + J V_\theta J', \qquad J = -(H + S)^{-1} \frac{\partial^2 \rho}{\partial\beta \partial\theta},$$ with \(V_\theta\) the variance of the estimated hyperparameters on their own free scale. It is the delta method applied to the map from the hyperparameter to the penalized mode (Wood, Pya and Safken, 2016), and the matrix that mgcv returns as unconditional = TRUE. The correction is positive semi-definite, so \(V'\) is never narrower than \(V_b\). It matters where a smoothing parameter is poorly determined, and it affects the penalized coordinates much more than the unpenalized ones. It requires the curvature of the outer criterion, which the two conditional matrices do not read, so unconditional_vcov() is more expensive than the other two conventions.

Where no hyperparameter was estimated by a differentiable criterion there is nothing to propagate, the correction is exactly zero and unconditional_vcov() returns \(V_b\) itself. Where a hyperparameter was estimated and the curvature of the criterion cannot be read at the fitted point, the conditional matrix is returned with a warning, so that the narrower matrix is not mistaken for the wider one. Where the curvature can be read for only some of the hyperparameters, the correction is a lower bound and a warning states it. See hyper_correction().

A coefficient that a kinked penalty has set to zero has NA in its row and column. At zero the penalty is not twice differentiable, so \(S\) does not exist there and the curvature cannot be read. The coefficients that a lasso or an MCP leaves non-zero have a variance, which is conditional on that selection; summary.StatmodFit() reports this in a note. Away from zero the lasso contributes nothing to \(S\), and SCAD and MCP contribute a negative curvature on their concave part, which makes the variance of a coefficient there larger than that of the likelihood alone. For these penalties \(V_b\) is therefore not the posterior variance under the corresponding prior, because a curvature read at the mode does not include the mass that the prior puts near zero.

The coefficients that the marginal criterion of reml() or ml() estimates take the curvature of that criterion in the Bayesian and the unconditional matrices, and the criterion reads the information of its own information argument. The information of vcov_type selects the matrix used as \(H\) everywhere else, in the sandwich of the frequentist matrix and in the penalized block of the other two.

The information of vcov_type selects the matrix used as \(H\). Its default is NULL, which is resolved for each fit by the family of the fit with the rule of distributions7::vcov.distrib_fit(): the matrix is distributions7::observed_info(), the curvature of the likelihood at the data in hand, when the log-likelihood is twice differentiable in every parameter of the family (every distributions7::params_order() is at least 2), and distributions7::expected_info() with method = NULL, for the whole matrix, otherwise. The choice does not depend on the information with which the fit was computed (inner_information of statmod()). An object in information overrides the rule. distributions7::expected_info() selects the Fisher information, the information averaged over the model. The two agree asymptotically and not in a sample. A model that carries a structural term is always inverted on the observed information, because a filter and a mixture over states do not have an expected information. summary.StatmodFit() states the matrix when it is not the observed one.

The observed information is singular where the second derivative of the log-likelihood in a coefficient is zero at the estimates, as for the location of a Laplace response. The family has a kink in that parameter, so the default NULL reads the expected information, which is finite there, and the variance is available. With information = observed_info() the rows and columns of the coordinates that it does not identify are missing, as described above for a flat direction.

The method of distributions7::expected_info() selects how the expected information is obtained. With method = NULL the closed form of the family is used where the family has one, and distributions7::expect_opg(), the outer product of the observed scores, which costs one gradient, otherwise. distributions7::expect_integrate() evaluates the expectation itself, a sum over the support for a discrete family and a quadrature for a continuous one, and is orders of magnitude more expensive; distributions7::expect_mc() simulates it. distributions7::expected_derivative_methods compares the three methods.

References

Wood, S. N., Pya, N. and Safken, B. (2016). Smoothing parameter and model selection for general smooth models. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 111(516), 1548–1563.

See also

vcov_method for the three conventions side by side, confint.StatmodFit(), summary.StatmodFit(), hyper_correction(), which builds the third matrix's correction

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(80))
dd$y <- 1 + 2 * dd$x + rnorm(80, sd = 0.4)
fit <- statmod(y ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd)
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))
#>    mu:(Intercept)              mu:x sigma:(Intercept) 
#>        0.08770104        0.14865515        0.08006408 

# With a penalized term the three differ for a penalized coefficient, and
# the widest is the one that does not read the smoothing parameter as known.
ds <- data.frame(x = runif(200))
ds$y <- sin(2 * pi * ds$x) + rnorm(200, sd = 0.3)
fs <- statmod(y ~ s(x, bspline_smooth(k = 10)), distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), ds)
vapply(list(frequentist_vcov(), bayesian_vcov(), unconditional_vcov()),
       function(ty) sqrt(diag(vcov(fs, vcov_type = ty)))[["mu:s(x).z2"]], 0)
#> [1] 0.06510115 0.06553290 0.06625519

# the information is chosen inside the convention
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit, vcov_type = bayesian_vcov(
  information = distributions7::expected_info()))))
#>    mu:(Intercept)              mu:x sigma:(Intercept) 
#>        0.08770104        0.14865515        0.08006408
